1. Use diagnosis to choose practice

Start by finding the skills you need to practice. Year 12 builds on the earlier units, so try the 20-minute diagnostic on your own before you run code or read the answers.

For each question, record your answer and how confident you feel. Use the questions you found difficult to choose optional practice. You do not need a score or readiness grade.

Download diagnostic Separate answers

In this example, you count invented observations that meet a minimum value. You will revisit types, comparisons, loops, functions, files and tests before working with more complex data structures.

2. Choose and trace loop forms

A fixed loop has an agreed iteration count; a pre-test loop checks before its body and may run zero times; a post-test loop checks after its body and runs at least once. Python has no dedicated do/while statement: an unconditional loop with a condition and break after the body models the post-test behaviour.

# Fixed count: zero iterations when n == 0
for i in range(n):
    print(i)

# Pre-test: may execute zero times
remaining = n
while remaining > 0:
    remaining -= 1

# Post-test equivalent: body executes at least once
attempts = 0
while True:
    attempts += 1
    if attempts >= n:
        break

Trace n=0 and n=3. The fixed/pre-test forms execute 0/0 or 3/3 bodies; the post-test form executes 1 or 3. Do not move its test above the body if the requirement says “ask at least once”. In illustrative pseudocode, REPEAT body UNTIL finished terminates when finished is true; WHILE condition continues while condition is true. Keep termination polarity explicit. Formal SCSA syntax verification remains separate.

3. Retrieve types, operators and Boolean precedence

Choose a data type by asking what the value means:

  • Use an integer for a count.
  • Use a float for an approximate measurement. Python stores floats with finite binary precision, so some decimal values cannot be stored exactly.
  • Use a string for an identifier such as "007" when the leading zeros matter. Converting it to an integer loses that formatting.
  • Use a Boolean for a true/false state.

Be careful when reading a Boolean from text. The string "False" is nonempty, so bool(text) treats it as true. Check for agreed input words and convert them explicitly.

7 / 2       # 3.5
7 // 2      # 3 (extra Python floor-division operator)
7 % 2       # 1
"7" + "2"   # "72"
7 >= 7      # True

# Python Boolean precedence: not, then and, then or
allowed = not blocked and trained or supervisor
strict = not blocked and (trained or supervisor)

Arithmetic comes before comparisons. Among the Boolean operators, not has higher priority than and; and has higher priority than or. Add parentheses to make your intended grouping clear.

Use blocked=True, trained=False and supervisor=True in the example. The result of allowed is True because supervisor can override the blocked condition. The result of strict is False because its grouping never allows a blocked person.

Try all eight combinations of the three Boolean inputs before you choose an expression. Python’s and and or operators can return one of their operands rather than a Boolean; these examples use Boolean inputs deliberately.

Foundation repair workbook · Explained answers · Offline reference. Embed these targeted retrieval tasks in the existing week 1 diagnosis/repair lessons; choose from the earlier tasks rather than adding lessons.

4. State the contract before writing code

Count every observation at least the supplied minimum. Equality counts; repeated values are separate observations; an empty list returns zero. For the counting function, values and minimum are assumed non-negative integers. Convert/validate input separately.

Example: [3, 5, 0, 8], minimum 5, returns 2. Compare [4, 5, 6] at minimum 5: two qualify. A strict-greater requirement would instead give one. Translate the wording before choosing the operator.

count = 0
FOR EACH value IN values
    IF value >= minimum THEN
        count = count + 1
    END IF
END FOR
RETURN count

5. Trace and isolate faults

For [3, 5, 0, 8] at minimum 5, count progresses 0 → 1 → 1 → 2. The accumulator starts at zero and changes only for qualifying values.

A strict > condition is a logic error for this contract. Indexing values[i] using range(len(values)+1) eventually uses index len(values), causing IndexError. Repair one fault at a time, compare actual with expected output and test the boundary again.

A missing colon or incorrect indentation can prevent parsing; a conversion or indexing error happens during execution; a plausible wrong count may run without an exception. Use traces, breakpoints or carefully placed diagnostic output to isolate the cause.

6. Separate validation, processing and display

Keep input checking separate from the calculation. input() gives you text. Convert suitable integer text with int, then check the allowed range. For example, int("5.0") raises ValueError, while a converted negative number fails the range check.

Our parser returns an integer when the input is valid and None when it is not. Zero is a valid integer here. Check rejection with value is None, not not value, because the second condition also treats zero as false.

Pass the checked value to the counting function. It returns a result; the mainline then displays that result.

A parameter is a name used inside a function. Giving it the same name as a caller’s variable does not automatically replace that caller’s value. Next week, you will explore this distinction with mutable structures.

Use the separate unfinished scaffold before reading the solution. A NotImplementedError marks a deliberate stub, not a completed function.

7. Compare development processes

A linear process moves through planned stages; stable requirements can support clear checkpoints, while late changes can require expensive rework. An iterative process revisits a solution through feedback; it helps refine uncertain needs, but needs priorities and version discipline. Neither removes the need for requirements, design, testing or evaluation.

Apply investigate → design → develop → evaluate to the counter. Then an organiser changes “at least” to “strictly greater”. Record the changed criterion, algorithm, boundary tests and version. Compare how each process accommodates that change; do not claim every project needs the same process.

8. Preserve versions and prove recovery

Keep meaningful known-good versions with a short record of requirement, change and passing tests. Version control tracks history; a backup provides another recoverable copy. Copies kept only on the same disk do not protect against losing that disk.

Use your school-approved storage and workflow. Restore a selected practice version into a separate folder, run its known tests and explain which requirement it implements. Preserve current work. A backup file’s presence does not prove that recovery has been checked.

Text-file revision: w creates/truncates, a appends. Check paths and existing work before writing. Detailed file operations are in the Unit 1 files chapter.

def count_at_least(values, minimum):
    if minimum < 0:
        raise ValueError("Minimum must be non-negative")
    count = 0
    for value in values:
        if value >= minimum:
            count += 1
    return count
for values, minimum in [([], 5), ([4, 5, 5], 5), ([0], 0)]:
    print(count_at_least(values, minimum))
Show expected output after your prediction
0
2
1

Worked Python example

Predict the result first, then run and modify the downloaded file in your Python environment.

"""Unit 3 Week 1: non-negative integer input and threshold counting.
count_at_least assumes values and minimum are non-negative integers.
The functions do not change the input list. Python 3; no extra packages.
"""

def parse_non_negative_integer(text):
    """Return a non-negative int or None; text comes from input()."""
    try:
        value = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        return None
    if value < 0:
        return None
    return value


def count_at_least(values, minimum):
    """Count every value >= minimum, including duplicates and the boundary."""
    count = 0
    for value in values:
        if value >= minimum:
            count += 1
    return count


def main():
    values = [3, 5, 0, 8]
    minimum = 5
    print(f"At least {minimum}: {count_at_least(values, minimum)}")
    for text in ["0", "5", "-1", "five", "5.0"]:
        value = parse_non_negative_integer(text)
        if value is None:
            print(f"{text!r}: rejected")
        else:
            print(f"{text!r}: accepted {value}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Practice and explain

Trace

What count is returned for [5,5] at minimum 5?

Show explained answer

Two. Duplicate observations are separate values, and both meet equality.

Validate

Why is if not value wrong for this parser?

Show explained answer

Zero is falsey but valid. Use value is None to identify rejection.

Distinguish

Does returning a value automatically change an outside variable with the same name?

Show explained answer

No. A return supplies a result; the caller must use/assign it as needed.

Recover

Does a same-disk snapshot guarantee recovery after disk loss?

Show explained answer

No. Backup placement and a tested restore matter; version history and backup serve related but different purposes.

Check your understanding

The parser returns 0 for valid zero and None for invalid input. Which condition correctly identifies rejection?

not value value is None value == 0

Quick-check answer and explanation

value is None

None is the rejection sentinel. Zero is a valid value even though it is falsey.

1. Choose the structure for the question

Start with the question you need the data to answer. If you need the item at a position, use a sequence. If you need a value by a label, such as a workshop name, consider a dictionary.

  • A one-dimensional array uses one position to identify an item.
  • A two-dimensional array uses a row and a column.
  • A dictionary maps each unique key to a value.

Here, Python lists model arrays, and lists of lists model two-dimensional arrays. They can grow or shrink; they are not fixed-size typed arrays.

Picture the invented workshop data as a grid: two rows for workshops and three columns for days. You can then use a dictionary to label each workshop’s total.

These structures hold data in memory. They do not provide the enforced foreign-key relationships of a relational database.

2. Read and update a two-dimensional grid

bookings = [[2, 0, 1], [0, 4, 0]]
print(bookings[1][1])  # 4
bookings[0][2] = 3

Indices start at zero. The first index selects a row; the second selects a cell in that row. Two rows have indices 0–1; three columns have indices 0–2. Python permits negative indices, but the booking interface deliberately rejects them. Lists of lists can be ragged; our grid contract requires equal row lengths.

Workshop / rowDay 0Day 1Day 2
Python / 0201
Robotics / 1040

3. Traverse rows and columns

totals = []
for row in bookings:
    total = 0
    for value in row:
        total = total + value
    totals.append(total)

To find each workshop’s total, work through one row at a time:

  1. Set that row’s accumulator to zero inside the outer loop.
  2. Add each value in the row.
  3. Store the completed total, then move to the next row.

The original grid gives row totals [3, 4]. To find the total for day 1 instead, take row[1] from every row: 0 + 4 = 4. The index 1 selects the second day.

SET totals TO empty array
FOR EACH row IN bookings
    SET total TO 0
    FOR EACH value IN row
        SET total TO total + value
    END FOR
    APPEND total TO totals
END FOR

This language-neutral pseudocode mirrors the algorithm. Follow the current SCSA support booklet when practicing course conventions.

4. Build and use a dictionary

totals = {"Python": 3, "Robotics": 4}
totals["Python"] = 5
totals["Networks"] = 0
for label, total in totals.items():
    print(label, total)
if "Security" in totals:
    print(totals["Security"])
else:
    print("Unknown workshop")
del totals["Networks"]

A repeated key replaces its previous value; it does not create a second entry. Keys must be hashable: strings and integers work; lists do not. Values may themselves be lists or dictionaries. A missing key accessed with square brackets raises KeyError. Use membership or get() deliberately; get(key, 0) can conceal a missing record when zero is a valid result. Dictionaries preserve insertion order, but that order is not a numeric index or an automatic sort.

5. Parameters: mutation and rebinding

def change(number, values):
    number = number + 1
    values.append(9)
    values = [100]

count = 3
items = [1, 2]
change(count, items)
print(count)  # 3
print(items)  # [1, 2, 9]

Follow the names and objects separately. When you call a Python function, its parameter becomes a local name for the object you supplied. Python calls this passing arguments by assignment.

  • number + 1 creates a new integer because integers are immutable. Assigning it to number changes the local binding.
  • append changes the existing list. A caller referring to that list sees the change too.
  • values = [100] makes values refer to a different list locally. It does not replace the caller’s list.

In the general value model, a procedure receives a copy of a value. In the reference model, it can affect referenced caller data. Use these models to discuss the course terminology, but do not describe Python simply as “all pass by reference”: that does not explain its mutation and rebinding behaviour.

A name can be local to a function while the object it refers to is shared with the caller. Scope tells you where a name is available; mutability tells you whether an object can change.

If you want the caller to replace a value, return the new value and assign the result explicitly in the caller.

Python FAQ: argument passing. Curriculum: 2026 Year 12 syllabus, Unit 3 programming.

Visual walkthrough

Change the object or change the name?

Start with a caller list [1]. A parameter called values refers to that same list.

Pause and predict: After the final step, does the caller list become [100]?

Show the explanation

No. Rebinding values only changes the local name. The caller still refers to the original list [1, 7].

Try a small change: Replace append with values = values + [7]. Explain why the caller would now keep [1].

6. Avoid shared rows and shallow-copy traps

bad = [[0] * 3] * 2
bad[0][0] = 7
print(bad)  # [[7, 0, 0], [7, 0, 0]]

good = []
for row in range(2):
    good.append([0] * 3)
copy = [row[:] for row in good]
copy[0][0] = 7
print(good)  # [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]

Multiplication in bad repeats references to one inner list. Create each row independently. good[:] copies only the outer list, so inner rows remain shared. Copying each row is sufficient here because the cells are immutable numbers; deeper nested mutable objects need a different copy strategy.

Use the worked functions below. The contract accepts numeric grid cells, unique string labels and integer dimensions/indices/place counts; it does not validate arbitrary object types. book mutates its input deliberately and returns None; row_totals and labelled_totals create new results without changing the grid. Empty grids produce [] and {}. A zero-column grid is permitted, but no booking can be made into it.

Predict the output: [[2, 0, 1], [0, 4, 0]], then {'Python': 3, 'Robotics': 4}. Record expected and actual results before changing the code.

8. Scope and Python argument binding

LIMIT = 5
def change(number, values):
    number = number + LIMIT
    values.append(number)
    values = [99]
    return number

number = 2
values = [1]
result = change(number, values)
print(number, values, result, LIMIT)

Predict output: 2 [1, 7] 7 5. LIMIT is a module-level name read by the function; number and values are local parameter names. Local rebinding of number does not replace the caller’s number. append mutates the shared list object; rebinding values to a new list does not redirect the caller’s values. The caller receives the result only because it assigns the returned value.

Python passes arguments by assignment. A parameter becomes another name for the supplied object. This is often called object sharing. Changing a shared list can be visible to the caller. Rebinding a parameter to a different object does not rebind the caller’s name.

Use the trace above when explaining value and reference terminology. Python does not switch to a different calling mechanism for integers and lists. Follow which names refer to which objects, and whether an operation changes an object or rebinds a name.

Scope reminder: assigning to a name inside a function normally makes that name local, unless it is declared global or nonlocal. Reading that local name before assigning a value can raise UnboundLocalError. Prefer clear parameters and returned results to changing global state.

Transfer: change values.append(number) to values = values + [number]. Now the caller’s list remains [1], because concatenation creates a new list and the local name is rebound. Write the before/after reference explanation and a fresh scalar/list/dictionary example. Scope practice. Use existing week 2 parameter/copy practice time.

Sources: Python scope and aliasing and Python function arguments/control flow.

9. Convention-focused transfer

The SCSA guidance uses = for assignment and == for equality, with explicit block endings. Earlier illustrative algorithms focus on logic; their None/-1 contracts must be preserved when translating. Use the convention clinic and independent evidence tasks for a source-checked notation exercise. The booklet does not prescribe one compulsory pseudocode grammar.

10. Choose dictionaries for labelled lookup and grids for position

Choose a structure from the operations the solution must support. A list of rows can hold equipment records, but a search by EquipmentID must locate the matching row before accessing its count. A dictionary keyed by EquipmentID makes the lookup intention explicit and replaces unexplained column numbers with meaningful field names.

NeedDictionary benefit or limit2D list benefit or limit
Find a record by a unique IDDirect key-based access; membership and get make missing cases explicitUsually scan rows unless another index is maintained
Read a map tile at row and columnPossible, but compound keys add unnecessary representation choicesNatural position-based access such as grid[row][column]
Keep record fields understandableNamed fields reduce reliance on column-number conventionsColumn meanings must be documented and used consistently
Store repeated labelsKeys must be unique; an assignment to an existing key replaces its valueRows can contain repeated labels; the design must define which row is intended

For ID lookup, a hash-based dictionary typically avoids a full row scan; it is not a promise that dictionaries are always faster or smaller. A grid already provides direct row/column access and often suits spatial traversal. Dictionaries carry representation overhead. Dictionary insertion order is retained in current Python, but keys are not automatically sorted. A dictionary is not a relational database: it does not automatically enforce foreign keys or prevent unsuitable updates.

Make a missing ID different from a present ID whose count is zero. Use membership when that distinction matters. Keys must be hashable; a mutable list is not a suitable dictionary key. Keep the chosen unique-ID rule in the design and test duplicate insertion explicitly.

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Replace one positional equipment row with named dictionary fields. Complete a missing-ID branch and demonstrate that 0 available items is not treated as an unknown ID.
  2. Independent transfer: Choose structures for an 8 × 10 game map and an item catalogue keyed by unique ID. Write add_item so a duplicate ID is rejected rather than silently overwritten. Test an existing zero-valued item, unknown ID and duplicate ID.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Given a new problem, justify the structure using access operations, uniqueness, missing cases and traversal, rather than saying a dictionary is always better.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

E02 exists and has 0 available. get('E99') returns None in this example. A grid suits map coordinates; a dictionary suits catalogue IDs. The duplicate check must happen before assignment, and rejecting a duplicate must preserve the earlier record. Do not use if catalogue.get(id) as the only existence check when legitimate stored values can be false-like.

  3. Delayed retrieval: Return after another topic and attempt a changed case without viewing the worked explanation. Explain what transferred and what still needs support.

Worked Python example

Predict the result first, then run and modify the downloaded file in your Python environment.

"""Synthetic workshop bookings: independent rows and explicit mutation."""
def make_grid(rows, columns):
    if rows < 0 or columns < 0:
        raise ValueError("Dimensions must be non-negative")
    grid = []
    for row in range(rows):
        grid.append([0] * columns)
    return grid

def row_totals(grid):
    totals = []
    for row in grid:
        total = 0
        for value in row:
            total += value
        totals.append(total)
    return totals

def book(grid, workshop, day, places):
    # Contract: rectangular grid; integer indexes/places (not booleans).
    # Bad indexes or negative places raise ValueError before mutation.
    if not 0 <= workshop < len(grid):
        raise ValueError("Unknown workshop")
    if not 0 <= day < len(grid[workshop]) or places < 0:
        raise ValueError("Invalid day or places")
    grid[workshop][day] += places

def labelled_totals(grid, labels):
    # Labels are unique strings, one per row; grid contains numbers.
    if len(labels) != len(grid) or len(set(labels)) != len(labels):
        raise ValueError("One unique label is required per row")
    totals = row_totals(grid)
    report = {}
    for index in range(len(labels)):
        report[labels[index]] = totals[index]
    return report

if __name__ == "__main__":
    bookings = make_grid(2, 3)
    book(bookings, 0, 0, 2)
    book(bookings, 0, 2, 1)
    book(bookings, 1, 1, 4)
    print(bookings)
    print(labelled_totals(bookings, ["Python", "Robotics"]))

Practice and explain

TRACE

For [[2, 0, 1], [0, 4, 0]], what are grid[0][2] and the row totals?

Show explained answer

1 and [3, 4]. Select row 0 before column 2; reset the accumulator for each row.

DIAGNOSE

Why does [[0] * 3] * 2 change both rows after one cell assignment?

Show explained answer

Both outer entries reference the same inner list. Create a new inner list on each iteration.

EXPLAIN

A function appends to a list and then assigns its parameter to []. What does the caller see?

Show explained answer

The append remains visible in the shared list. Rebinding the local parameter does not replace the caller’s variable.

CHOOSE

A report must retrieve a workshop total by its name. Which structure fits?

Show explained answer

A dictionary keyed by workshop name; keys must be unique. An indexed grid fits the day-by-workshop counts.

Your practical task

Implement the booking report from the starter. Add a day_totals function, leaving the input unchanged. Specify the rectangular-grid contract. Test an empty grid, zero columns, ordinary data, duplicate labels and invalid indices. Explain one deliberate mutation and one rebinding.

def book(grid, workshop, day, places):

    # Bad indexes or negative places raise ValueError before mutation.

def labelled_totals(grid, labels):

    if len(labels) != len(grid) or len(set(labels)) != len(labels):

if __name__ == "__main__":

    book(bookings, 0, 2, 1)
    book(bookings, 1, 1, 4)

def day_totals(grid):
    # Contract: rectangular grid of numbers; input is not mutated.
    if not grid:
        return []
    totals = []
    for column in range(len(grid[0])):
        total = 0
        for row in grid:
            total += row[column]
        totals.append(total)
    return totals

Check your understanding

Which statement explains why a list append inside a function remains visible to the caller?

All local names become global. The parameter and caller name refer to the same mutable list. Assigning a new list to the parameter replaces the caller variable.

Quick-check answer and explanation

The parameter and caller name refer to the same mutable list.

append mutates the shared list object. Assignment to the parameter would only rebind the local name.

1. Specify what finding means

Decide what a successful search should return before you write it. In this chapter, the input is a list of integer IDs and an integer target. The result is the target’s zero-based index, or None if it is absent. Neither function changes the list.

Duplicates need a clear rule. Linear search returns the first matching index. The binary search used here returns a matching index, which might be a later duplicate.

These agreed input, output and change rules form the function’s contract.

Index 0 is a successful result. Use result is not None, not if result, to distinguish it from failure. A returned -1 would also need deliberate handling because Python treats -1 as the last index.

2. Linear search: check in order

Start at index 0, compare each item with the target and stop at the first match. If every item has been checked, return None. Sorting is unnecessary.

FUNCTION linearSearch(values, target)
    FOR index FROM 0 TO LENGTH(values) - 1
        IF values[index] = target THEN
            RETURN index
        END IF
    END FOR
    RETURN NONE
END FUNCTION

The FOR range is inclusive in this illustrative pseudocode; an empty list performs zero iterations. Python range(len(values)) excludes its upper endpoint. These are language-neutral algorithm notes; use current SCSA conventions for course notation practice.

For [101, 104, 108, 112, 117, 123, 130], searching 117 checks indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and returns 4 after five item probes.

3. Binary search: discard half

First, check the requirement for this version of binary search: the values must be in ascending order using the same comparison rule as the search. This is its precondition—something that must be true before it starts.

low and high are indices, not the values stored at those positions. Both endpoints are included. For seven items, start at low = 0 and high = 6.

Compute mid as (low + high) // 2. For non-negative indices, // discards any fractional half: with bounds 0 and 5, mid is 2, not 2.5. Use values[mid] to read the item to compare.

  1. Set low and high to include the first and last candidate positions.
  2. Find the middle index using integer division.
  3. If the middle value matches, return its index.
  4. If it is smaller than the target, keep the right half and set low to mid + 1. Otherwise, keep the left half and set high to mid − 1.
  5. Repeat until you find a match or low exceeds high.

The +1 and −1 exclude the item you have just checked. That makes the remaining interval smaller each time.

FUNCTION binarySearch(values, target)
    SET low TO 0
    SET high TO LENGTH(values) - 1
    WHILE low <= high
        SET mid TO (low + high) DIV 2
        IF values[mid] = target THEN
            RETURN mid
        ELSE IF values[mid] < target THEN
            SET low TO mid + 1
        ELSE
            SET high TO mid - 1
        END IF
    END WHILE
    RETURN NONE
END FUNCTION

For an empty list, high starts at −1. The loop therefore stops without accessing an item.

For sorted input, a target that is present must remain between low and high after each step. This continuing rule is the invariant that lets you discard half the candidates safely.

The search-time bound does not include sorting the list or checking its order. Doing either inside every search would add extra work.

4. Desk-check the bounds

Find 117 in [101, 104, 108, 112, 117, 123, 130]. Before each probe, write down low and high. Then calculate mid, inspect that value and decide which bound changes.

The table records the bounds before each probe, so you can check how one row leads to the next.

ProbelowhighmidvalueAction
1063112low = 4
2465123high = 4
3444117return 4

Now search for 119. The first two probes are the same. The third checks index 4, whose value is 117. Set low to 5; high is still 4. No candidates remain, so return None.

Check two common mistakes:

  • low < high would stop before checking a final single candidate. Use low <= high for this algorithm.
  • low = mid can leave the same interval to be checked again. Exclude the tested middle item so the interval keeps shrinking.

Three probes find 117

Use ascending IDs [101, 104, 108, 112, 117, 123, 130]. Record the bounds before each probe.

Pause and predict: If the target changes to 119, what happens after the third probe?

Show the explanation

Index 4 contains 117, which is smaller than 119. Set low to 5. Now low exceeds high (4), so return None.

Try a small change: Use target 101. Trace the new bounds and explain why a successful index 0 must not be mistaken for failure.

5. Compare growth, not just a stopwatch

Big O describes an asymptotic upper bound on resource growth as input size n increases. For these iterative implementations with constant-time indexing and integer comparisons, the usual tight worst-case time bounds are O(n) for linear search and O(log n) for binary search. Both can find their first probed item in O(1); best-case speed does not change the worst-case classification. Both use O(1) extra space.

n itemsLinear: max probesBinary: max probes
884
16165
32326
1024102411

For n > 0, binary search makes at most floor(log2(n)) + 1 item probes; an empty list makes zero. Doubling n doubles linear worst-case probes but adds one binary probe. One binary probe may evaluate equality and then ordering: item probes are not identical to counts of individual Boolean comparisons. Use a consistent measure in your experiment.

These bounds concern the search, not preparation. Sorting a fresh list just for one lookup can outweigh the saving; sorting also changes index meanings. For many lookups in already sorted data, binary search is attractive. Timing small inputs reflects overhead and the environment as well as algorithm growth.

6. Choose and test a search

Choose linear search for a short unsorted list or when the first original occurrence matters. Choose binary search for repeated lookups in sorted indexed data when any matching occurrence is sufficient. A dictionary can suit lookup by a unique ID, but that is a different structure and contract.

Do not silently sort the caller’s list: a result would then refer to the reordered list. If a separate sorted view is required, retain original identifiers/index mappings. A sortedness check is O(n), so keep the validated-data boundary separate from a repeated-search routine.

Test empty, singleton hit/miss, index 0, last item, absent below/between/above values and duplicates. A deliberately unsorted example such as [3, 1, 2] with target 3 demonstrates a violated binary-search precondition: linear search returns 0 while this binary search returns None. That is not a correctness test of binary search on valid input.

Worked Python example

"""Search integer IDs. Return an index, or None when absent."""
def linear_search(values, target):
    for index in range(len(values)):
        if values[index] == target:
            return index
    return None

def binary_search(values, target):
    # Precondition: values is sorted in ascending order.
    low = 0
    high = len(values) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if values[mid] == target:
            return mid
        elif values[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ids = [101, 104, 108, 112, 117, 123, 130]
    for target in [101, 117, 999]:
        print(target, linear_search(ids, target), binary_search(ids, target))

Practice and explain

TRACE

How many item probes does each algorithm need to find 117 in the seven-ID example?

Show explained answer

Linear: 5, returning index 4. Binary: 3, probing indices 3, 5, 4 and returning 4.

BOUNDARY

Why must the binary loop include low == high?

Show explained answer

One candidate remains when the bounds are equal. Excluding equality can miss a valid result.

CONTRACT

Can binary search guarantee the first occurrence in [2, 2, 2]?

Show explained answer

This implementation returns index 1, a matching occurrence. Linear search returns index 0. Finding the first by binary search needs a modified algorithm.

GROWTH

What happens to worst-case probes when input grows from 16 to 32 items?

Show explained answer

Linear doubles from 16 to 32. Binary increases from 5 to 6. Count item probes consistently.

"""Search integer IDs. Return an index, or None when absent."""
def linear_search(values, target):

def binary_search(values, target):

if __name__ == "__main__":

def probe_count(values, target, binary=False):
    # Count examined items, not equality/ordering operations or elapsed time.
    probes = 0
    if not binary:
        for index in range(len(values)):
            probes += 1
            if values[index] == target:
                return index, probes
        return None, probes
    low, high = 0, len(values) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        probes += 1
        if values[mid] == target:
            return mid, probes
        elif values[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return None, probes

The ordering lets the algorithm safely discard half the interval. Odd sizes and duplicate values are allowed.

1. Define the sorting contract

A pass is one run through an outer loop’s work. A prefix is the start of a list; a suffix is its end. Each sorting algorithm gradually fixes one of these regions. Keep a copy of the original data so you can check that no value was lost.

Decide what the sort is allowed to change and what it must preserve. Here, each function puts a list of integers into ascending order. Every value must remain, including every copy of a duplicate.

These functions mutate the list: they change the list you pass in. Their return value is a comparison count, not the sorted list.

Count only comparisons between data values. Leave index and boundary checks out of this count so that you compare all three algorithms using the same measure.

working = original[:]
comparisons = bubble_sort(working)
# working is now sorted; original is unchanged.

In the example, you make a copy before calling the sort. The sort itself uses constant extra space, but your copy adds O(n) space and copying work to the whole task.

After calling bubble_sort(working), inspect working for the ordered values. Do not write working = bubble_sort(working): that would bind working to the returned integer count.

2. Bubble sort: move the largest to the end

Work from left to right, comparing one neighbouring pair at a time. Swap a pair only when its values are out of order.

After a complete pass, the largest remaining value is at the right end. That completed part is the sorted suffix. Shorten the next pass so you do not compare it again.

  1. Reset swapped at the start of each pass.
  2. Compare and, where needed, swap the neighbouring pairs.
  3. If no swaps occurred during the whole pass, stop: the list is sorted.
FUNCTION bubbleSort(values)
    FOR end FROM LENGTH(values) - 1 DOWN TO 1
        SET swapped TO FALSE
        FOR index FROM 0 TO end - 1
            IF values[index] > values[index + 1] THEN
                SWAP values[index], values[index + 1]
                SET swapped TO TRUE
            END IF
        END FOR
        IF swapped = FALSE THEN
            EXIT FOR
        END IF
    END FOR
END FUNCTION

These illustrative pseudocode ranges include both endpoints; impossible ranges perform zero iterations. Python range excludes its stop value. The pseudocode shows the sorting logic; the Python implementation additionally counts key comparisons. Follow current SCSA support conventions in course notation practice.

Worked walkthrough

Zoom in on one bubble pass

Start with [5, 2, 4, 1]. Compare neighbouring values from left to right.

Pause and predict: Is [2, 4, 1, 5] fully sorted? Which part can the next pass leave alone?

Show the explanation

It is not fully sorted: 4 is still before 1. The last value, 5, is fixed, so the next pass checks only the first three positions.

Try a small change: Trace the first pass for [1, 2, 4, 5]. Explain why a complete pass with no swaps allows early exit.

Visual walkthrough

One bubble pass

Start with [5, 2, 4, 1]. Each row shows the list after a neighbouring-pair comparison.

Pause and predict: Is the whole list sorted after these three comparisons?

Show the explanation

No. The 5 is in its final position, but [2, 4, 1] is not sorted. The next pass excludes the fixed 5.

Try a small change: Predict the second complete pass. Explain why [2, 1, 4, 5] still needs another pass.

3. Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix

Imagine inserting a card into a hand of cards that is already ordered. Insertion sort uses the same idea. The ordered part at the start is called the sorted prefix.

  1. Treat the first item as the initial sorted prefix.
  2. Save the next item as key.
  3. Shift larger items in the prefix one position to the right.
  4. Put the saved key into the gap, then repeat with the next item.

After each insertion, the prefix is sorted. The remaining suffix has not been processed yet. Save key before shifting, because a shift could overwrite its original position.

FUNCTION insertionSort(values)
    FOR index FROM 1 TO LENGTH(values) - 1
        SET key TO values[index]
        SET position TO index - 1
        WHILE position >= 0
            IF values[position] <= key THEN
                EXIT WHILE
            END IF
            SET values[position + 1] TO values[position]
            SET position TO position - 1
        END WHILE
        SET values[position + 1] TO key
    END FOR
END FUNCTION

The boundary check occurs before reading values[position], so a negative index is not accidentally treated as a valid Python element. A shift copies one item; it is not the same operation as swapping two items.

Worked walkthrough

Keep the saved key while shifting

After the first insertion, the list is [2, 5, 4, 1]. The next key is 4.

Pause and predict: Has the algorithm lost 4 after the shift?

Show the explanation

No. The separate key variable still holds 4. It is placed into the gap after the larger values move right.

Try a small change: Insert 1 into [2, 4, 5]. Record each shift and keep key visible beside the list.

4. Selection sort: place the smallest remaining item

Scan the unsorted suffix to find the index of its minimum. Swap that item into the next position only after finishing the scan. The sorted prefix grows by one. Track the smallest index, rather than confusing a minimum value with a position. This version avoids swapping an item with itself.

FUNCTION selectionSort(values)
    FOR start FROM 0 TO LENGTH(values) - 2
        SET smallest TO start
        FOR index FROM start + 1 TO LENGTH(values) - 1
            IF values[index] < values[smallest] THEN
                SET smallest TO index
            END IF
        END FOR
        IF smallest != start THEN
            SWAP values[start], values[smallest]
        END IF
    END FOR
END FUNCTION

Even an already sorted list still needs the minimum scan on every pass. One long-distance swap can reorder items with equal keys, unlike the adjacent swaps in this bubble sort.

Worked walkthrough

Finish the scan before swapping

Start with [5, 2, 4, 1]. Remember the position of the smallest value seen so far.

Pause and predict: Should you swap 5 and 2 as soon as you inspect index 1?

Show the explanation

Not in this selection-sort version. Finish finding the smallest value, then make the one final swap for this pass.

Try a small change: Trace the first pass for [4, 3, 2, 1]. Separate the minimum-index updates from the final swap.

Use [5, 2, 4, 1]. Each row below records the list after one complete outer-loop pass. “Comparisons” refers to key comparisons made by the worked Python functions during that pass.

PassBubble / comparisonsInsertion / comparisonsSelection / comparisons
1[2, 4, 1, 5] / 3[2, 5, 4, 1] / 1[1, 2, 4, 5] / 3
2[2, 1, 4, 5] / 2[2, 4, 5, 1] / 2[1, 2, 4, 5] / 2
3[1, 2, 4, 5] / 1[1, 2, 4, 5] / 3[1, 2, 4, 5] / 1

All three make six key comparisons on this particular input. This does not prove equal performance on other inputs. For a desk check, also record the inner index, compared values, swap/shift decision and the current sorted region.

6. Compare growth and the work being counted

Big O describes a growth bound as input size n increases, not a precise time in seconds. Under constant-time integer comparisons/indexing, these implementations have the following usual tight time bounds. Best cases refer to already sorted input; empty and singleton inputs need zero key comparisons.

AlgorithmBest timeWorst timeExtra space inside routine
Bubble, with early exitO(n)O(n²)O(1)
InsertionO(n)O(n²)O(1)
SelectionO(n²)O(n²)O(1)

For n ≥ 1, sorted input needs n − 1 key comparisons in this bubble and insertion sort. Selection always makes n(n − 1)/2. Strictly reverse-sorted distinct values make all three perform n(n − 1)/2 key comparisons. Optimised bubble therefore differs from a version that always completes every pass.

nSorted bubble/insertionSelection (any order) / reverse all three
8728
1615120
3231496

Quadratic worst-case work grows roughly fourfold when n doubles for large n. Comparison counts alone omit movement: selection makes at most n − 1 swaps, whereas reverse input makes bubble perform n(n − 1)/2 swaps and insertion perform that many shifts, plus key placements. They are different operations with different costs. Use both ordering and size when designing experiments.

7. Equal keys, stability and a practical choice

A stable sort retains the original relative order of records with equal sort keys. For example, [(2, A), (2, B), (1, C)] becomes [(1, C), (2, A), (2, B)] under a stable sort by the numeric key. Our bubble rule swaps only greater values; insertion shifts only greater values, so both are stable. This selection strategy is not: its first swap puts C before B before A, reversing A and B. The record labels are explanatory tags; the worked code sorts integers.

For a short or nearly sorted list, insertion is often a useful teaching choice. If minimising swaps matters and stability is unnecessary, selection offers few swaps but still scans quadratically. Bubble is straightforward to trace but can require many swaps. No choice is universally fastest: justify requirements, data order, size and movement costs.

For ordinary application code, Python provides sorted(values) for a new list and values.sort() to change the existing list and return None. Both are stable and support keys. They are not these three teaching algorithms. Practice writing and tracing the required algorithms here; use built-in sorting when the application requirements allow it.

8. Test, explain and connect back to searching

Check ascending order and that every original value is still present the same number of times (the same multiset). Test [], [7], sorted, reverse, duplicates, all equal and negative values. Test both the intentional mutation and the unchanged original when a caller makes a copy. Ascending output alone is insufficient: a broken sort might drop a repeated value.

Sort a separate ID list, then reuse last chapter’s binary search. State that its returned index belongs to the sorted list. Include sorting cost in a one-off lookup; do not describe the whole sort-and-search task as O(log n). These three sorts have O(n²) worst-case time.

Worked Python example

Predict the result first, then run and modify the downloaded file in your Python environment.

"""Sort integer lists in place; return the number of key comparisons.
Index/bound checks are not counted. These are teaching implementations.
"""
def bubble_sort(values):
    comparisons = 0
    for end in range(len(values) - 1, 0, -1):
        swapped = False
        for index in range(end):
            comparisons += 1
            if values[index] > values[index + 1]:
                values[index], values[index + 1] = values[index + 1], values[index]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:
            break
    return comparisons

def insertion_sort(values):
    comparisons = 0
    for index in range(1, len(values)):
        key = values[index]
        position = index - 1
        while position >= 0:
            comparisons += 1
            if values[position] <= key:
                break
            values[position + 1] = values[position]
            position -= 1
        values[position + 1] = key
    return comparisons

def selection_sort(values):
    comparisons = 0
    for start in range(len(values) - 1):
        smallest = start
        for index in range(start + 1, len(values)):
            comparisons += 1
            if values[index] < values[smallest]:
                smallest = index
        if smallest != start:
            values[start], values[smallest] = values[smallest], values[start]
    return comparisons

if __name__ == "__main__":
    original = [5, 2, 4, 1]
    for sort in [bubble_sort, insertion_sort, selection_sort]:
        working = original[:]
        count = sort(working)
        print(sort.__name__, working, count)
    print("Original:", original)

Practice and explain

TRACE

What is the list after the first complete pass of each algorithm on [5, 2, 4, 1]?

Show explained answer

Bubble [2,4,1,5]; insertion [2,5,4,1]; selection [1,2,4,5]. Each strategy establishes a different sorted region.

DIAGNOSE

Why must insertion sort save key before shifting values?

Show explained answer

The shift can overwrite its original cell. Saving key preserves the item that must be inserted into the final gap.

GROWTH

Why is best-case selection sort still O(n²)?

Show explained answer

It scans the entire remaining suffix to find a minimum on every pass, even if no swaps are needed.

CONTRACT

Why is result = bubble_sort(values) not a sorted list in this chapter?

Show explained answer

The function mutates values and returns an integer comparison count. Inspect values for the ordered data.

TEST

Why must a sort test check duplicates as well as ascending order?

Show explained answer

A result can be ascending while losing values. Compare the output multiset or a trusted sorted reference to ensure every occurrence remains.

"""Sort integer lists in place; return the number of key comparisons.
Index/bound checks are not counted. These are teaching implementations.
"""
def bubble_sort(values):
    comparisons = 0
    for end in range(len(values) - 1, 0, -1):
        swapped = False
        for index in range(end):
            comparisons += 1
            if values[index] > values[index + 1]:
                values[index], values[index + 1] = values[index + 1], values[index]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:
            break
    return comparisons

def insertion_sort(values):
    comparisons = 0
    for index in range(1, len(values)):
        key = values[index]
        position = index - 1
        while position >= 0:
            comparisons += 1
            if values[position] <= key:
                break
            values[position + 1] = values[position]
            position -= 1
        values[position + 1] = key
    return comparisons

def selection_sort(values):
    comparisons = 0
    for start in range(len(values) - 1):
        smallest = start
        for index in range(start + 1, len(values)):
            comparisons += 1
            if values[index] < values[smallest]:
                smallest = index
        if smallest != start:
            values[start], values[smallest] = values[smallest], values[start]
    return comparisons

if __name__ == "__main__":
    original = [5, 2, 4, 1]
    for sort in [bubble_sort, insertion_sort, selection_sort]:
        working = original[:]
        count = sort(working)
        print(sort.__name__, working, count)
    print("Original:", original)


def comparison_report():
    for size in [8, 16, 32]:
        datasets = {
            "sorted": list(range(size)),
            "reverse": list(range(size - 1, -1, -1)),
        }
        for order, original in datasets.items():
            for sort in [bubble_sort, insertion_sort, selection_sort]:
                working = original[:]
                count = sort(working)
                assert working == sorted(original)
                print(size, order, sort.__name__, count)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    comparison_report()

Compare the logic and tests, not just the spelling of variable names.

Check your understanding

Why can this bubble sort stop after a complete pass with no swaps?

Every neighbouring pair in the remaining region is already in order, and the suffix is already fixed. It has completed exactly half its passes. No swaps means all values are equal.

Quick-check answer and explanation

Every neighbouring pair in the remaining region is already in order, and the suffix is already fixed.

An ordered remaining region plus the already sorted suffix means the whole list is sorted. The values need not be equal.

Chapter recap

Bubble builds a sorted suffix, insertion grows a prefix by shifting, and selection places successive minima. Count a defined operation, preserve duplicates, distinguish mutation from return values and justify choices against the data and requirements.

  2. Lesson 2: model insertion shifts and saved key; trace prefix growth; implement and compare sorted/reverse data.
  3. Lesson 3: model minimum selection; implement selection sort; test empty/singleton/duplicate/negative cases and mutation contracts.
  4. Lesson 4: compare key counts and Big O; discuss stability/movement; justify a scenario choice and connect to binary search. All practical work fits inside these four lessons.

1. From separate data to an object

Think about one stock item, such as a camera. You need to store its ID, name, total units and units on loan. You also need operations to lend units, accept returns and report availability.

The stored values are its state: what the object knows right now. The operations are its behaviour: what it can do. A class keeps related state and behaviour together, rather than leaving you to coordinate separate lists, dictionaries and functions.

Equipment is the class: the definition of this kind of object. A particular camera or tripod is an instance created from that class. Each instance has its own state.

An attribute stores a value on an object. A method implements an operation. Use object-oriented design when this grouping makes responsibilities clearer; a small calculation may still need only a function.

2. Design the class before coding

This original stock-count model uses synthetic equipment only. It does not record borrowers, dates, reservations or authorisation, and it cannot verify who returned an item. Those responsibilities belong in a fuller booking design later.

MemberResponsibility / contract
_equipment_id, _nameNon-empty strings; surrounding whitespace removed
_total, _on_loanNon-negative integer stock; on-loan initially 0
get_id(), get_name()Return identifying strings; do not change state
available()Return total − on-loan; do not change state
lend(quantity=1)Increase on-loan if enough units; return True or False
return_units(quantity=1)Decrease on-loan if enough are currently loaned; return True or False

The invariant is 0 ≤ on_loan ≤ total. Positive integer quantities are required; booleans and non-integers are rejected. Invalid input raises ValueError before a change. A valid quantity that exceeds availability or units on loan returns False with state unchanged. Choose one clear contract and test it consistently.

3. Instantiate and initialise

camera = Equipment("E01", "Camera", 2)
tripod = Equipment("E02", "Tripod", 1)
print(camera.available())  # 2
print(tripod.available())  # 1

Call Equipment(...) to create an instance. Python then runs __init__ to give that instance its starting state. This starting process is called initialisation.

You may hear this discussed as construction. More precisely, __init__ works on an instance that has already been created. It must return None; it does not return the new object itself.

Use self to refer to the instance receiving the method call. It is the conventional first parameter of an instance method.

For example, self._total = total stores the supplied total on that instance. The name total by itself is a local parameter.

When you call camera.available(), Python passes camera as self automatically. You do not pass it a second time.

Read camera.lend() from left to right: find the object named camera, then call its lend method. Inside that call, self refers to that camera object. An attribute such as self._on_loan belongs to that instance.

4. Methods: queries and commands

A query reports state without changing it; available() is a query. A command changes state deliberately; lend() and return_units() are commands that also report whether the change succeeded. Avoid input() or print() inside these methods so their logic can be reused and tested separately from the interface.

camera = Equipment("E01", "Camera", 2)
print(camera.lend())       # True; available now 1
print(camera.lend(2))      # False; still 1
print(camera.return_units())  # True; available now 2

The default quantity of 1 lets lend() request one unit; lend(2) supplies an explicit argument. available() can be called from another method as self.available(). Missing parentheses refer to the method rather than calling it.

5. Encapsulation and abstraction

Ask a camera to lend a unit by calling lend(). Keep the stock update and its checks inside the object’s methods. Grouping the data with the methods that keep it valid is encapsulation.

You can also call available() without repeating the stock arithmetic or knowing every field used inside the object. This useful interface hides unnecessary detail: it is abstraction.

The public interface tells you what an operation does. The implementation contains the steps that make it happen.

In Python, a leading underscore marks an internal detail by convention. It does not block access. For example, camera._on_loan = 99 bypasses our checks and can break the stock invariant.

Double-underscore name mangling is not a security boundary either. This example relies on callers using the intended interface; it does not control real users’ access.

Properties can provide managed attributes in a later design. You do not need them for this opening example.

Visual walkthrough

Protect the stock rule

A camera starts with total stock 2 and no units on loan. The public methods check changes.

Pause and predict: Why does the failed lend(2) leave availability at 1?

Show the explanation

There is only one available unit. The method rejects the request before changing stock, preserving the invariant.

Try a small change: Try returning one more unit after the final row. Predict the result and explain which state must remain unchanged.

6. Separate instances, shared aliases and class attributes

first = Equipment("E01", "Camera", 2)
second = Equipment("E02", "Tripod", 1)
alias = first
alias.lend()
print(first.available())   # 1
print(second.available())  # 1
print(alias is first)      # True

Assignment alias = first does not copy the instance. Both names refer to one object, so a method call through either changes the same state. A new Equipment(...) call makes a separate instance. The class does not enforce catalogue-wide ID uniqueness; a catalogue must check that rule separately.

class BadLog:
    events = []  # Shared mutable class attribute

class GoodLog:
    def __init__(self):
        self.events = []  # New list for each instance

A class attribute belongs to the class and can be shared by its instances. An instance attribute set through self belongs to that instance. For separate histories, create the list inside __init__; a shared class-level list makes one item’s appended event appear in other items’ histories. Intentional shared constants can be class attributes, but per-item mutable state should be independent.

Object diagram

Two names can lead to one object

Create a two-unit camera and a one-unit tripod, then assign alias = camera.

Pause and predict: After alias.lend(), what do camera.available() and tripod.available() return?

Show the explanation

Both return 1. The camera now has one of its two units on loan. The separate tripod still has its original one unit available.

Try a small change: Call camera.return_units() next. Explain why alias.available() changes but tripod.available() does not.

Move the stock operations from a dictionary-and-functions version into Equipment. Retain the requirements and compare both versions with the same test cases; adding class syntax alone is not evidence of an improved design.

Extension: store Equipment instances in a list. Write find_equipment(items, equipment_id) as a linear search returning the matching object or None. Require unique IDs in the catalogue. The returned object is shared with the list, so lending through it updates that catalogue item. 9. Public, protected and private: intention, interface and Python conventions

Encapsulation groups state with the operations that maintain its rules. Information hiding reduces a caller's dependence on representation. For a ticket pool, the important invariant is that remaining places cannot become negative through a valid booking operation. Choose access according to responsibilities, not because every attribute needs a getter and setter.

Design termIntended accessTypical Python notationImportant limit
PublicCallers use the supported interfacename, book(), available()Document its contract; public need not mean every change is sensible
ProtectedClass implementation and cooperating subclasses_label or _x conventionally marks non-public statePython has no enforced protected access modifier
PrivateImplementation detail of the defining class__remaining triggers name manglingMangling helps avoid accidental clashes; it is not access security

The plus, hash and minus signs in a conceptual class diagram commonly denote public, protected and private visibility respectively. In Python, ordinary attributes remain accessible; a single underscore is a cooperation convention. Double-leading underscores rewrite the name inside a class. An informed caller can still reach a mangled name, so neither convention protects secrets from hostile code.

The supported book method checks the quantity before changing state. Reading via available exposes the result without asking the caller to understand the stored attribute. The example deliberately shows a mangled access to explain its limit, not to recommend it. Compare the benefits: callers have one reliable rule-enforcing entry point, internal representation can change behind the interface, and tests can target observable behaviour.

This section connects requested design vocabulary to Python's actual behaviour. Access-modifier syntax and property machinery from other languages are not additional project requirements.

Pause and predict

After a pool of 3 books 2 places, what should happen to an attempted booking of 2 more? Does name mangling make the remaining count secret?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download encapsulation.py

class TicketPool:
    def __init__(self, name, capacity):
        if isinstance(capacity, bool) or not isinstance(capacity, int) or capacity < 0:
            raise ValueError("Capacity must be a non-negative whole number")
        self.name = name             # public interface
        self._label = "places"      # non-public convention
        self.__remaining = capacity  # name mangled
    def available(self):
        return self.__remaining
    def book(self, quantity):
        if isinstance(quantity, bool) or not isinstance(quantity, int) or quantity <= 0 or quantity > self.__remaining:
            raise ValueError("Invalid booking quantity")
        self.__remaining -= quantity
pool = TicketPool("Robotics", 3)
print(pool.name, pool.available())
pool.book(2)
print(pool.available())
try:
    pool.book(2)
except ValueError:
    print("rejected", pool.available())
try:
    print(pool.__remaining)
except AttributeError:
    print("ordinary double-underscore access fails")
print("mangled access is possible", pool._TicketPool__remaining)
Show expected output after your prediction
Robotics 3
1
rejected 1
ordinary double-underscore access fails
mangled access is possible 1

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download inheritance_conventions.py

class Actor:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self._x = x
    def position(self):
        return self._x
    def move(self, distance):
        self._x += distance
    def update(self):
        self.move(0)
class Hazard(Actor):
    def update(self):
        self.move(1)
first, second = Hazard(0), Hazard(0)
first.update()
print(first.position(), second.position())
# A leading underscore requests cooperation; it does not prevent access.
print(first._x)
Show expected output after your prediction
1 0
1

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Annotate each public method and internal attribute. Draw the invariant before/after each operation. Explain why the rejected booking must leave 1 place rather than changing state first.
  2. Independent transfer: Add a cancellation method that cannot increase remaining places above the original capacity. Specify valid/invalid inputs and test both rejection and unchanged state. Decide which capacity field is an implementation detail and justify the public interface.
  3. Delayed retrieval: From a blank page, contrast design intention with enforcement for name, _name and __name. Explain why authorisation for a real system is separate from these naming conventions.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The first booking leaves 1. The second is rejected and must leave 1. Ordinary pool.__remaining access fails, but the mangled name remains accessible. For cancellation, store the original capacity, validate the requested positive quantity and upper bound before mutation, and check that a rejected cancellation leaves the previous value intact. Equivalent documented class designs are acceptable.

Worked Python example

Predict the result first, then run and modify the downloaded file in your Python environment.

"""Synthetic stock counts, not a borrower or calendar booking system."""
class Equipment:
    def __init__(self, equipment_id, name, total):
        if not isinstance(equipment_id, str) or not equipment_id.strip():
            raise ValueError("A non-empty equipment ID is required")
        if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip():
            raise ValueError("A non-empty name is required")
        if type(total) is not int or total < 0:
            raise ValueError("Total must be a non-negative integer")
        self._equipment_id = equipment_id.strip()
        self._name = name.strip()
        self._total = total
        self._on_loan = 0

    def get_id(self):
        return self._equipment_id

    def get_name(self):
        return self._name

    def available(self):
        return self._total - self._on_loan

    def lend(self, quantity=1):
        if type(quantity) is not int or quantity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Quantity must be a positive integer")
        if quantity > self.available():
            return False
        self._on_loan += quantity
        return True

    def return_units(self, quantity=1):
        if type(quantity) is not int or quantity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Quantity must be a positive integer")
        if quantity > self._on_loan:
            return False
        self._on_loan -= quantity
        return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    camera = Equipment("E01", "Camera", 2)
    tripod = Equipment("E02", "Tripod", 1)
    print(camera.get_id(), camera.available())
    print(camera.lend(), camera.available())
    print(camera.lend(2), camera.available())
    print(camera.return_units(), camera.available())
    print(tripod.get_id(), tripod.available())

Practice and explain

IDENTIFY

In camera = Equipment("E01", "Camera", 2), identify the class and instance.

Show explained answer

Equipment is the class. The new object referred to by camera is an instance. E01, Camera and 2 are arguments used during initialisation.

TRACE

After a two-unit camera lends one unit then rejects lend(2), how many remain?

Show explained answer

One. The first operation increases on-loan to 1; the excessive request returns False without changing it.

EXPLAIN

Does an underscore make _on_loan impossible to access outside the class?

Show explained answer

No. It marks an internal detail by convention. Direct assignment can bypass validation; encapsulation here relies on using the intended methods.

ALIAS

Does alias = camera make a second independent camera?

Show explained answer

No. It binds another name to the same object. Changes through either name are visible through the other.

DIAGNOSE

Why should a separate history list be created as self.events = [] in __init__?

Show explained answer

Each instance receives its own list. A mutable list at class scope would be shared when accessed and mutated by instances.

Your practical task

Implement Equipment from the starter and verify the interface contracts. Test boundary and rejected operations, two independent instances and an alias. Refactor the supplied procedural version while retaining its behaviour. Extend with a linear object lookup and an availability report, then explain why lookup returns a shared object but the report is a snapshot of values.

def find_equipment(items, equipment_id):
    # IDs must be unique in the supplied catalogue. No list mutation.
    for item in items:
        if item.get_id() == equipment_id:
            return item
    return None

def availability_report(items):
    report = []
    for item in items:
        report.append({"id": item.get_id(), "name": item.get_name(),
                       "available": item.available()})
    return report

if __name__ == "__main__":
    catalogue = [Equipment("E01", "Camera", 2),
                 Equipment("E02", "Tripod", 1)]
    found = find_equipment(catalogue, "E01")
    if found is not None:
        found.lend()
    print(availability_report(catalogue))

Compare the logic and tests, not just the spelling of variable names.

Check your understanding

What does camera.lend() pass automatically as the method’s self argument?

The Equipment class definition. The instance referred to by camera. The number of units available.

Quick-check answer and explanation

The instance referred to by camera.

The bound method receives the camera instance as self; the default quantity is supplied separately.

Chapter recap

A class defines a kind of object; an instance holds particular state. Methods use self, queries report state and commands change it. Initialise instance data deliberately, respect the interface and test both valid changes and unchanged rejected operations.

  2. Lesson 2: explain __init__/self; implement queries and commands; trace boundaries and rejected operations.

  4. Lesson 4: independently complete/test the class, object lookup and report; peer-review contracts and evidence. Extension work can be scaled to diagnostic readiness; no extra major project is introduced.

UNIT 3 / WEEK 6 / CHAPTER 6

Extending object-oriented design

Reuse a common interface, specialise behaviour and explain which method a mixed collection calls.

PYTHON 3 / INHERITANCE CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Extend a superclass with subclass attributes and initialisation.
  • Override methods while preserving shared contracts.
  • Demonstrate polymorphism and distinguish it from abstraction.
  • Choose inheritance or composition and test inherited behaviour.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Extend a responsibility, not just a name

A Camera is a kind of Equipment. So is a Projector. Both still need the stock operations from week 5, but each adds its own preparation data and behaviour.

Equipment is the superclass. Camera and Projector are subclasses: they inherit common operations and can extend or override selected behaviour.

A subclass instance must still work wherever the Equipment stock contract is expected. Being more specialised should not break valid calls to that interface.

Now compare a Kit that contains several items. A kit has Equipment items; it is not itself one of those stock items. Store the items as attributes or in a list. This relationship is composition.

Choose inheritance for a suitable “is a kind of” relationship, not just because two things share a field or because it saves a few lines.

2. Initialise common state with super()

class Camera(Equipment):
    def __init__(self, equipment_id, name, total, charge):
        # Validate charge first.
        super().__init__(equipment_id, name, total)
        self._charge = charge

This abbreviated design sketch omits validation; the worked implementation includes it. Camera(Equipment) declares the inheritance relationship. The subclass __init__ does not automatically run the superclass __init__. super().__init__(...) reuses its validation and stock initialisation for the same instance, then the subclass stores its extra state. It does not construct a separate Equipment object.

In this single-inheritance hierarchy, super() continues method lookup to the superclass. More generally it follows Python’s method resolution order; it is not a command to copy all parent fields. If the subclass defines no __init__, it inherits the existing initialiser, as the AudioRecorder extension demonstrates.

Follow one object: creating a Camera starts its subclass initialisation. super().__init__(...) sets up the common stock attributes on that same instance. The subclass then adds its camera-specific charge attribute. You finish with one camera object containing both kinds of state.

3. Override behaviour while keeping the interface

def preparation(self):
    if self._charge < 20:
        return "Charge the camera"
    return "Check the lens"

Call preparation() on Equipment and you get a general message. Camera and Projector define their own versions of that same method, using the same caller-facing arguments. This replacement of inherited behaviour is overriding.

The subclasses do not replace lend(), so that inherited method remains available.

When you override a method, keep the meaning, result type and valid calls that its users expect. The shared report would break if one version required an extra argument or returned an unrelated kind of result.

Do not try to create signature-based overloading by defining the same method name twice with different parameter counts in one Python class. The later definition replaces the earlier name.

Keep three ideas separate: inherit means reuse an available superclass method; override means supply a subclass version; polymorphism means the same caller-facing operation can use different implementations for different objects. Use the class diagram to locate the relationship, then the call trace to follow what runs.

4. Polymorphism: one call, different implementations

for item in items:
    print(item.get_id(), item.preparation())

Call preparation() on each item in the mixed collection. Python selects the method for the object receiving that call: Camera gives its camera message, Projector its projector message, and Equipment its general message.

The report needs only that shared interface. It does not need an if/elif branch for every subclass. Add another kind of equipment that follows the same interface, and the reporting loop can stay unchanged.

The same call producing suitable behaviour for different objects is polymorphism. Merely creating subclasses does not demonstrate it; show which implementation each call uses.

This example uses a shared superclass. Python can also use another object with compatible get_id() and preparation() methods, even if it does not inherit from Equipment.

Worked walkthrough

Follow the receiver of each method call

In the report loop, item refers to a different object on each pass. The call stays item.preparation().

Pause and predict: Must preparation_report gain a new if branch when AudioRecorder is added?

Show the explanation

No. If the new class supports the same required methods and result types, the existing report can call them unchanged.

Try a small change: Explain which method AudioRecorder overrides and which stock methods it inherits.

Visual walkthrough

One call, three receivers

The report calls item.preparation() without checking each subclass itself.

Pause and predict: An AudioRecorder supplies compatible get_id() and preparation() methods. Must the reporting loop gain a new type-check branch?

Show the explanation

No. The loop can keep calling the common methods. Each receiver supplies its own implementation; that is the polymorphic behaviour.

Try a small change: Explain what would break if AudioRecorder.preparation() required an extra argument from the caller.

5. Abstraction and a consistent stock contract

The report needs an ID and a preparation message; it does not need to know how charge or lamp hours are stored. That interface is an abstraction. Encapsulation keeps each implementation’s state and operations together. Inheritance organises shared and specialised behaviour. Polymorphism lets a shared call select the appropriate implementation. Explain these four ideas separately.

Equipment is a concrete class in this model: it can be instantiated and its preparation method works. Abstraction does not require making an abstract base class. Python’s abc tools can enforce abstract-method requirements in a later extension, but are not needed to understand this interface.

All classes retain the stock invariant 0 ≤ on_loan ≤ total. We do not override lending to add an undocumented camera-only rejection. Preparation is a query and never changes stock. Each subclass has its own instance data; underscore attributes remain a convention, not enforced privacy.

6. Trace dispatch and boundary changes

Our fictional classroom model uses charge < 20 and lamp hours ≥ 1000 to choose messages. These invented thresholds are for tracing code, not manufacturer guidance. Charge must be an integer from 0 to 100; hours must be a non-negative integer. Booleans and non-integers are rejected with ValueError before state changes.

Object / beforeMethod selectedMessageChange / next message
E01 Camera, charge 19Camera.preparationCharge the cameraset_charge(20) → Check the lens
E02 Projector, hours 999Projector.preparationCheck the ventilationadd_usage(1) → Arrange a projector check
E03 EquipmentEquipment.preparationCheck the item before useNo change

The intervening camera.lend() returns True and leaves one unit available. Both preparation changes leave that availability unchanged. Trace the actual receiver and selected method as well as the returned string.

7. Test common and specialised behaviour

Run the inherited lending/return tests on Equipment, Camera and Projector, not only on the superclass. Check zero stock, exact stock, insufficient stock, excessive return and invalid quantities. Then test camera charge 0, 19, 20, 100 and rejected −1/101/non-integer; test projector hours 0, 999, 1000 and rejected negative/non-integer input. Invalid setters must leave the instance unchanged.

Test a mixed report, an empty list and a new subtype using the existing report unchanged. Confirm preparation queries do not mutate state and that changes to one instance do not affect another. A successful demonstration output is useful but does not replace boundary tests.

8. Practice, then try it independently

Extend the supplied base class using inheritance, initialisation and overriding. Add AudioRecorder with its own preparation query while keeping the inherited stock contract. Use the mixed report to demonstrate polymorphism. Explain a separate composition design for a kit containing items.

9. Test an overridden method and independent objects

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. The code is ordinary Python 3 and runs offline. Work in a disposable learning folder. These are ungraded practice examples, not additional assessment requirements.

Pause and predict

Does updating first move second? Does the underscore block access?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download inheritance_conventions.py

class Actor:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self._x = x
    def position(self):
        return self._x
    def move(self, distance):
        self._x += distance
    def update(self):
        self.move(0)
class Hazard(Actor):
    def update(self):
        self.move(1)
first, second = Hazard(0), Hazard(0)
first.update()
print(first.position(), second.position())
# A leading underscore requests cooperation; it does not prevent access.
print(first._x)
Show expected output after your prediction
1 0
1
