Find this chapter’s activities and downloads.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Start with measurable requirements

Start by listing what the network must do. Who will use it? Which services and locations must it connect? How much traffic and growth must it support? What access restrictions and downtime limits matter?

These answers are your requirements. Choose a design, then test whether it meets them. A higher advertised link rate alone does not prove that the design is better.

Continue the fictional media-centre plan. The groups have 50 Media endpoints, 25 Staff endpoints, 12 Devices endpoints and 6 Visitors endpoints. Each subnet also needs a gateway.

  • Staff may print to Devices.
  • Media may use the internet.
  • Visitors may use the internet, but must not start connections to internal groups.
  • Every group needs the agreed DHCP and DNS services.

Add a protected administration path and state who may use it. Treat this as a classroom model, not a description of your school’s network.

Performance requirement: 20 Media clients each need 8 Mbit/s concurrently across their shared uplink. State whether that traffic stays local or crosses the internet before choosing the link. Security requirement: demonstrate both permitted services and blocked cross-group attempts.

2. Choose components by their role

ComponentRole and design consequence
Transmission mediaCopper/fibre carry signals; wireless uses radio. Consider supported distance/rate, interference, mobility, installation and cost. Fibre is useful for distance and electrical isolation; wireless airtime is shared.
Modem / service terminationConnects to an access service using its required signalling. An optical network terminal is not simply a telephone-line modem. Provider access equipment and home all-in-one devices can combine roles.
Layer 2 switchForwards frames using MAC information within a VLAN. A VLAN is a separate logical broadcast domain; separate switch ports alone do not create separate broadcast domains.
Router / layer 3 switchRoutes IP packets between subnets. A multilayer switch can route too. Document where routing occurs and where access rules are enforced.
Default gatewayThe host’s route towards other networks, usually a router interface on its local subnet. Gateway describes a role; it need not be a separate box.
Wireless access pointConnects wireless clients to a LAN. It need not route or provide internet access itself. An SSID can map to a VLAN; a different SSID alone does not prove isolation.
FirewallEnforces traffic policy at defined boundaries; implementations can inspect several layers. A firewall is neither an automatic encryption service nor proof that every host is safe.

Explain each component’s main OSI role without claiming a multifunction appliance belongs exclusively to one layer. Layer 1 media, layer 2 switching and layer 3 routing are useful starting points. Firewalls can also make transport/application decisions.

3. Draw physical and logical topology

Draw the network from two viewpoints:

  • A physical diagram shows the equipment, ports, links and locations.
  • A logical diagram shows the subnets, VLANs, gateways, services and permitted paths.

One managed switch can carry several logical networks. Label the intermediary devices, representative end devices, link media and rates, prefixes, and routing/filtering point. Include a legend so the meaning does not depend on colour alone.

Ask what happens when a link or device fails. In a switched star, a failed access link usually affects that connection, but the central switch or uplink can be a single point of failure.

A hierarchical star supports more access switches, but the links collecting their traffic need enough capacity. Redundant paths can improve availability only when loop prevention, routing and failover are configured correctly. An extra cable alone is not enough.

Compare the cost, complexity and recovery time of each design.

The syllabus specifies Cisco conventions. Use the official Cisco topology icon reference for cloud, router, switch, firewall, server, PC and access-point symbols in the final student diagram. The original diagrams here explain the structure; they are not a certified substitute for that symbol set. Include a symbol-identification and redraw check in lesson 1.

4. Separate broadcast domains and enforce policy

In this design VLAN 10 is Media, VLAN 20 Staff, VLAN 30 Devices and VLAN 40 Visitors. Each uses its own IPv4 subnet. Access ports carry a selected VLAN; a configured trunk carries multiple VLANs to the routing/firewall device. Layer 2 broadcasts are normally contained within their VLAN; routers do not forward them as ordinary routed traffic. DHCP across a routing boundary may need an explicitly configured relay.

Subnetting is an addressing plan; VLAN membership is link-layer separation; routing and firewall rules govern traffic between groups. They work together but are not interchangeable. Once routing is enabled, separate VLANs do not automatically block cross-group access. Traffic between two hosts in the same VLAN may bypass the central firewall, requiring endpoint controls or other isolation if that traffic must be restricted.

VLAN / groupSubnetGatewayOrdinary capacity
10 / Media192.168.50.0/26192.168.50.162
20 / Staff192.168.50.64/27192.168.50.6530
30 / Devices192.168.50.96/28192.168.50.9714
40 / Visitors192.168.50.112/28192.168.50.11314

Keep 192.168.50.128/25 reserved. Gateways in this model are VLAN interfaces on the firewall/router, not invented addresses on a separate PC. NAT may translate private IPv4 addresses at the internet edge, but it is not encryption or a replacement for explicit filtering.

5. Write a service-specific traffic policy

Begin with the smallest set of required flows and deny other new inter-zone connections. Document source, destination, protocol/service, action and reason. Evaluate rule order; a broad early allow can defeat a later deny. Stateful return traffic for an allowed session is distinct from permission to initiate a new session in the opposite direction.

Initiating sourceDestination / serviceActionReason
MediaInternet / agreed web serviceAllowLearning resources
StaffDevice printer 192.168.50.98 / TCP 631AllowScenario uses IPP printing
VisitorsInternet / agreed web serviceAllowGuest access
VisitorsAny internal group / new sessionDenyProtect internal systems
Any groupAgreed DNS/DHCP serviceAllow narrowlyRequired infrastructure; specify local/relay path
Unlisted inter-zone flowAnyDenyDefault-deny policy

This is a requirements matrix, not a deployable firewall configuration. A real ruleset must specify actual destinations, DNS transports, DHCP broadcast/relay handling, IPv4/IPv6 and stateful return handling. TCP 443 is a conventional HTTPS service; HTTP/3 can use UDP 443. Our offline model deliberately simplifies web to TCP 443. Port numbers alone do not prove application identity or encryption.

Use separate guest access, appropriate wireless authentication/encryption, maintained software, restricted device management and physically secured equipment. Match controls to the risk and environment. Private addresses, hidden SSIDs and MAC filtering do not provide a complete security design. Record remaining risks and service dependencies.

Pause and predict: A visitor needs to open the media web service. Does that justify allowing every visitor connection to every staff device?

Show the explanation

No. Describe the required source, destination and service. Permit that flow in the practice policy and test an unrelated flow that should remain blocked. A rule allowing one service is not permission for all traffic.

Try a small change: Write one allowed test and one blocked test for your rule. Predict the result of each before using the supplied model.

6. Calculate capacity and identify bottlenecks

Bandwidth is link capacity; throughput is achieved transfer rate; latency is delay. Jitter is variation in delay. Compare measurements under stated loads. Units matter: eight bits make one byte, and this chapter uses decimal Mbit/s and MB.

20 clients × 8 Mbit/s = 160 Mbit/s demand
100 Mbit/s shared uplink: demand / capacity = 1.6 (160%)
Ideal equal-share ceiling = 100 / 20 = 5 Mbit/s per client
400 MB file × 8 / 100 Mbit/s = 32 seconds ideal minimum

A 1 Gbit/s uplink removes the stated 100 Mbit/s bottleneck, but does not guarantee each application rate. Protocol overhead, competing traffic, storage, firewall processing, wireless airtime and server capacity still matter. If this traffic crosses a 100 Mbit/s internet link, a faster local uplink leaves that external bottleneck in place. The file estimate excludes overhead and other activity.

For latency-sensitive calls, low and stable delay may matter more than bulk-transfer speed. QoS can prioritise selected traffic during contention; it does not create capacity. Compare wired stability with wireless mobility, and test peak concurrent use rather than one idle client.

7. Use ping and traceroute as evidence

Use ping to ask whether an ICMP echo reply comes back and to measure round-trip time (RTT). That is narrower than proving that a website works: ping does not test bulk bandwidth or authenticate a user.

If it times out, possible causes include filtering, a lost reply or an unavailable host or path. If an IP responds but its name cannot be resolved, check DNS. One observation suggests a next test; it does not establish the whole cause.

Windows tracert sends probes with increasing TTL or hop limits. Replies can reveal some routed hops, but not layer 2 switches.

An asterisk means that probe received no reply. If a later hop replies, forwarding still continued far enough to reach it. Other traceroute implementations can use different probe types.

Each hop’s RTT is measured from the source and back. Do not subtract adjacent RTTs and treat the result as a reliable delay for the link between them.

Synthetic example only — do not run against these documentation targets:
tracert -d 198.51.100.20
 1    1 ms   1 ms   1 ms   192.168.50.1
 2    *      *      *      Request timed out.
 3   12 ms  13 ms  12 ms   198.51.100.20

Hop 2 did not answer the probes, but the destination responded. This output alone does not show that hop 2 dropped ordinary forwarded traffic. A high RTT at one responding hop followed by lower later RTTs can reflect control-plane response priority rather than a path bottleneck.

In a teacher-controlled lab, practice with an explicitly assigned responding target. Windows forms: ping -n 4 TARGET and tracert -d TARGET. Record the target, timestamp, load, sent/received counts and RTTs, then state a limited conclusion. Use supplied synthetic logs when a lab is unavailable. Never treat a deliberately blocked guest-to-internal ping as a fault simply because it times out.

Visual walkthrough

A missing reply is a limited observation

Read the synthetic three-hop result before choosing a conclusion.

Pause and predict: Does the unanswered second hop prove that ordinary traffic stops there?

Show the explanation

No. The destination reply shows forwarding continued. Filtering, reply loss or response prioritisation can affect probe replies.

Try a small change: If ping succeeds but the web service fails, name one service or transport check that would help distinguish the cause.

8. Test, evaluate and revise the design

Write acceptance tests before changing the design: valid addressing, allowed services, blocked initiation, DNS/DHCP availability, performance under the required load, and recovery after an agreed failure. Distinguish predicted results, simulator observations and real measurements. Ping/traceroute evidence must be interpreted with filtering and probe limits in mind.

Use the offline Python model to predict the simplified traffic matrix and calculate capacity. It opens no sockets and changes no configuration. A passed prediction is not evidence that a deployed firewall enforces it. For an authorised lab or simulator, capture both allowed and denied outcomes, then compare with requirements. Record unresolved controls and a retest plan.

Practice and explain

SEGMENT

Do two VLANs automatically stop all traffic between their users?

Show explained answer

No. VLANs separate layer 2 broadcast domains, but routing and access rules determine cross-VLAN traffic.

CAPACITY

Twenty clients need 8 Mbit/s each over a 100 Mbit/s uplink. What is the problem?

Show explained answer

Demand is 160 Mbit/s, exceeding 100 Mbit/s. Ideal equal share is at most 5 Mbit/s before overhead.

EVIDENCE

Hop 2 times out, but hop 3 is the responding destination. Is the route broken at hop 2?

Show explained answer

The probe did not receive a response at hop 2. Later response shows traffic reached the destination; do not infer a forwarding failure from the asterisks alone.

POLICY

Why is a guest-to-internal ping timeout not sufficient proof of isolation?

Show explained answer

Only that probe lacked a reply. Test the required service policy and inspect evidence; other protocols or paths might still be allowed.

DESIGN

Why can a faster local switch leave internet downloads slow?

Show explained answer

An unchanged internet link, server, storage, wireless or firewall can remain the limiting resource. Identify the actual traffic path.

Your practical task

Use the media-centre brief to produce a Cisco-convention logical diagram and a physical link plan, a narrow traffic matrix, a capacity calculation and an acceptance-test table. Interpret the supplied logs and revise one design weakness. Practice ping/tracert only in the assigned lab.

Show illustrative answer / example

Allocate the four previous subnets to VLANs 10/20/30/40 with gateway interfaces at the routed firewall boundary. Allow required web/printing and infrastructure paths; deny other new cross-zone flows. A 100 Mbit/s uplink cannot meet 160 Mbit/s demand. Evaluate a faster uplink while checking the internet/server path. Validate positive and negative tests and retain uncertainty for ICMP timeouts.

Check your understanding

What actually enforces the guest-to-internal restriction in this routed design?

Giving the guest network a private IP prefix. A different SSID name by itself. Correctly placed and tested traffic rules at the relevant boundary.

Quick-check answer and explanation

Correctly placed and tested traffic rules at the relevant boundary.

Separate addressing and labels do not enforce the policy. Routing, filtering and the actual traffic path must be configured and tested.

Chapter recap

A diagram is a testable design. Addressing, VLAN membership, routing and service policy must agree. Capacity calculations expose bottlenecks; diagnostic probes support limited conclusions that require follow-up evidence.

  2. Lesson 2: VLANs/broadcast domains, gateways and service policy; test the simplified offline traffic matrix.
  3. Lesson 3: demand/bottleneck calculations, media/topology tradeoffs and capacity feedback.
  4. Lesson 4: interpret synthetic logs, practice ping/tracert in the assigned lab, evaluate and revise the design. Four lessons in week 13; practical work is embedded.

1. Diagnose before revising

Try the 12-question diagnostic without notes. Before you check each explanation, record how confident you are: low, medium or high.

Give extra attention to a confident wrong answer: you may be applying an incorrect rule. One correct answer is useful evidence, but it does not establish mastery.

For each error, record four things:

  1. What you thought.
  2. The corrected rule.
  3. The example or test that supports the correction.
  4. A fresh question you can try without looking at the answer.

Keep programming and networking evidence separate, while noticing how both use design and testing. These are original practice activities, not an official examination or a full syllabus audit.

FocusEvidence to produce
ProgrammingTrace state; justify key/order; repair a contract; test boundaries
Software designExplain objects/overriding; preserve invariants; record regression/version evidence
NetworksCalculate prefix/range; trace addresses/layers; justify capacity and policy
EvaluationDistinguish predictions from measurements; state limits and choose next test

2. Trace data structures and state

grid = [[0, 0] for _ in range(2)]
grid[0][1] = 3
alias = grid
copy = [row[:] for row in grid]
alias[1][0] = 4
copy[0][0] = 9
print(grid)
print(copy)

Predict both outputs before running. An alias binds another name to the same object. Copying each row separates the row lists here, but it is not a general deep copy of arbitrary nested mutable objects. Explain that limit with a counterexample containing a mutable object inside a row.

Compare the trace
grid: [[0, 3], [4, 0]]
copy: [[9, 3], [0, 0]]

The alias mutation updates grid. The copied row mutation does not. If row entries themselves were mutable lists, this one-level row copy would still share those entries.

Continue with dictionaries: an ID key must remain unique. Decide whether duplicate insertion is a rejection or an update before implementing it. A 2D availability grid and an ID dictionary solve different access problems; justify each from the required operations.

3. Connect sorting, searching and contracts

records = [("C03", 2), ("C01", 1), ("C02", 2)]
for i in range(1, len(records)):
    item = records[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and records[j][1] > item[1]:
        records[j + 1] = records[j]
        j -= 1
    records[j + 1] = item
print(records)

Look at the order after sorting. The quantities are ascending, and the two equal quantities keep their original order. This shows stability for this example.

Now ask whether the IDs are ascending. They are not, so you cannot apply ID binary search directly. Its required starting condition—the precondition—is order by the same key you will search.

def find_id(records, target):
    low, high = 0, len(records) - 1
    while low < high:  # deliberate fault
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if records[mid][0] == target:
            return mid
        if records[mid][0] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1

The faulty loop stops while one candidate still remains: low equals high. Repair that boundary, then trace a successful search in a one-item list.

Next, test empty input, an absent target, and targets at the first and last positions. Decide whether you need any matching index or the first duplicate. This exercise assumes unique IDs in ascending ID order.

Compare growth by counting the same operation in each algorithm. State what you count, such as an item probe.

Binary search grows logarithmically on a suitable sorted sequence, but arranging that sequence first takes work. Repeated unique-ID lookups may suit a dictionary better. You can keep a separate quantity-sorted view for display.

One timing result on a tiny input cannot show that an algorithm is always fastest.

4. Review objects and reliable changes

Return to the equipment-loan project. Separate the equipment object’s stock state from the system’s loan records. A successful loan cannot make stock negative; returning one active loan restores stock once; repeating a return must preserve the agreed state. Write expected results before running tests.

For a mixed collection of Camera and Projector objects, explain inherited common behaviour and overridden methods. Demonstrate polymorphism by calling the same method name through each object. Reassigning a local parameter differs from mutating the object it references; include this distinction in your trace.

Propose one maintenance change, such as a clearer rejection message, without adding a new project. Record the requirement, implementation version, failing example, fix and regression evidence. Use synthetic records; cite permitted external help, protect privacy and consider inclusive/ergonomic presentation. Passing a component test does not replace acceptance evidence for the whole user workflow.

5. Work an integrated network case

A Media client is 192.168.50.10/26, gateway 192.168.50.1. Staff uses .64/27, Devices .96/28 and Visitors .112/28. The printer is .98; the default-deny policy permits Staff printing but denies new Visitor-to-internal sessions. Keep the four previous gateway/subnet allocations.

QuestionExpected reasoning
Which block contains Media .10/26?Network .0, broadcast .63, ordinary hosts .1–.62,62 usable
Is printer .98 local to Media?No; .98 belongs to .96/28. Send towards gateway if an appropriate route/policy exists
Does another VLAN alone block printing?No. Routing/filtering enforce inter-zone permission
What happens to remote IP and local frame destination?Without NAT, remote IP remains; next-hop frame uses gateway MAC
20 × 8 Mbit/s over 100 Mbit/s?160 demand;100 bottleneck; identify local versus internet path
IPv6 2001:db8:50:1::70/64?128-bit notation; hexadecimal groups; no IPv4 subtract-two broadcast convention

Redraw the logical topology using the specified Cisco symbols, including intermediary and end devices, prefixes, gateway location, traffic-policy boundary and labelled links. The conceptual diagram in the previous chapter is a guide to structure; check symbol fidelity separately.

Choose TCP or UDP from application needs and explain the tradeoff. TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream, but is not automatic encryption. UDP does not supply TCP-style delivery/order guarantees; applications can build mechanisms above it. Do not describe every web application as TCP-only.

6. Interpret evidence and diagnose layers

Choose your next check from the observation:

  • Case A: ping to an assigned server IP works, but name resolution fails. Check DNS records and client configuration. The IP reply does not establish application health.
  • Case B: ping works, but a web connection fails. Check transport policy, the listening service and application or TLS conditions. Do not conclude that every network service is healthy.
  • Case C: a traceroute hop does not reply, but the destination does. Record the missing probe reply; it does not prove a broken forwarding link.
  • Case D: Visitor-to-Staff ping times out. Filtering is one explanation, but that alone does not show that every prohibited service or path is blocked.

Compare allowed and denied test results with the intended policy.

Every conclusion should cite an observation, acknowledge alternative explanations and propose a discriminating next test. Use teacher-assigned targets for live-tool practice. Supplied logs are synthetic and do not complete the live ping/traceroute skill by themselves.

Visual walkthrough

Match a next check to the symptom

A successful probe answers one question. Choose the next check from what still fails.

Pause and predict: Which card fits a server that replies by IP but whose hostname cannot be resolved?

Show the explanation

The first card. DNS records or client configuration are sensible next checks; the observation alone does not identify exactly which is wrong.

Try a small change: For the guest timeout, explain why testing an allowed service as well as a denied one gives more useful policy evidence.

9. Keep record identity separate from an index

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. The code is ordinary Python 3 and runs offline. Work in a disposable learning folder. These are ungraded practice examples, not additional assessment requirements.

Pause and predict

Is the index of 9 the same before and after sorting?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download sort_then_search.py

def find_first(values, target):
    for index, value in enumerate(values):
        if value == target:
            return index
    return -1
original = [9, 2, 7]
ordered = sorted(original)
print("original", original, find_first(original, 9))
print("ordered", ordered, find_first(ordered, 9))
# sorted is a library operation here; it is not an implementation of a taught sort.
Show expected output after your prediction
original [9, 2, 7] 0
ordered [2, 7, 9] 2

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Draw the two lists and annotate each index. Explain how returning an index into a changed list affects a caller.

  3. Delayed retrieval: After a gap, solve a changed version without copying the example. Explain one design decision and use a new test to demonstrate transfer.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

9 moves from index 0 to 2. An index belongs to a particular sequence state; it is not a permanent record ID.

Practice and explain

D1

Trace the grid/alias/copy example below. Explain why only one grid changes after copy[0][0] = 9.

Show explained answer

grid [[0,3],[4,0]]; copy [[9,3],[0,0]]. alias names the same outer list; copied rows are separate lists of immutable integers.

D2

What goes wrong with [[0,0]] * 2 when one row is changed?

Show explained answer

Both positions reference the same row list. A comprehension creates distinct rows.

D3

A dictionary maps unique equipment IDs to objects. What must happen before inserting a duplicate ID?

Show explained answer

Apply the contract: reject the duplicate or use an explicitly agreed update. Unchecked assignment replaces the existing value.

D4

Trace insertion sorting by the second tuple item. Why is C03 still before C02?

Show explained answer

Result C01(1), C03(2), C02(2). Strict > shifts only larger keys, preserving equal-key order.

D5

May binary search by ID be applied to that quantity-sorted result?

Show explained answer

No: it is not sorted by the searched ID key. Choose linear search, dictionary lookup or a separate ID-sorted index.

D6

Repair find_id and give a smallest revealing test.

Show explained answer

Use low <= high. One matching record is never checked by the faulty loop; also test empty, absent, first and last.

D7

Two objects inherit Equipment and override label(). What does calling item.label() through a mixed list illustrate?

Show explained answer

Polymorphism: method selection depends on the actual object. Inheritance reuses a common interface/behaviour; overriding supplies subclass behaviour.

D8

A return operation increments stock twice when the same loan is returned twice. What test and guard are needed?

Show explained answer

Return the same loan twice; second attempt must reject/no-op under the contract and leave stock/history consistent. Check active state before changing it.

D9

For host 192.168.50.70/27 give network, broadcast, ordinary capacity and a valid candidate gateway.

Show explained answer

Network .64, broadcast .95, capacity 30, candidate .65. It must actually be a router interface, not just fit arithmetically.

D10

Explain IP destination versus next-hop MAC when .70/27 sends to 198.51.100.20 through .65, with no NAT.

Show explained answer

IP destination remains the remote server; the local Ethernet frame targets the gateway MAC. Routing rebuilds link-layer headers for the next link.

D11

20 clients each require 8 Mbit/s through a 100 Mbit/s uplink. Can it meet demand?

Show explained answer

160 Mbit/s demand exceeds 100; ideal equal share 5 Mbit/s before overhead. Faster client ports alone do not repair the shared bottleneck.

D12

Traceroute has an unanswered middle hop but the destination responds. What can you conclude?

Show explained answer

That probe lacked a reply; later response shows the destination was reached. Do not infer forwarding failure at the unanswered hop alone.

Your practical task

Complete the diagnostic, repair and test the supplied search function, explain object invariants, solve the media-centre network case and attempt the optional mixed practice. Review your reasoning, correct two misconceptions and retry fresh questions.

Show illustrative answer / example

The grid/alias trace gives [[0,3],[4,0]] while the row copy gives [[9,3],[0,0]]. Stable quantity order is C01,C03,C02 and is unsuitable for ID binary search. Repair <= and test the final candidate. Network and performance conclusions must include prefix arithmetic, actual filtering location and the limits of probe evidence. Use the pack’s explanation points for the practice.

Check your understanding

Records are sorted by quantity. What must you check before binary searching by ID?

Nothing: any sorted list is suitable. The sequence is sorted by the same ID key used in the search. The quantities have no duplicates.

Quick-check answer and explanation

The sequence is sorted by the same ID key used in the search.

Binary search depends on the searched key being ordered consistently. Quantity order does not establish ID order.

Chapter recap

Good review produces evidence: a trace, a contract, a tested correction, an accurate network calculation and a limited conclusion. Use those results to choose the next task rather than rereading everything equally.

3. Work a state correction

counts = {"camera": 3, "projector": 1}
alias = counts
snapshot = counts.copy()
alias["camera"] -= 1
snapshot["projector"] = 9
print(counts)
print(snapshot)

Predict the final dictionaries before running the example. The alias is another name for the same dictionary. Updating the camera count through that name also changes counts.

The copied mapping is a separate dictionary. Assigning a new projector value in that copy does not change counts. This is enough independence here because the values are immutable integers.

A shallow copy copies the mapping, not every object stored inside it. If a value were a mutable list, both dictionaries would still refer to that list.

Compare and explain
counts: {'camera': 2, 'projector': 1}
snapshot: {'camera': 3, 'projector': 9}

Test the limit with a new example: make a dictionary whose value is a list, copy the dictionary, then append to the list.

Explain why both mappings show the appended value. Choose a copying strategy based on which objects must be independent. Do not assume copy() recursively duplicates nested objects.

Use the workbook’s shared-row repair and nested-copy question to demonstrate that your rule transfers beyond this one trace.

4. Make algorithm and object reasoning explicit

Sort X03:4, X01:2, X02:4 by quantity using stable insertion sort. The order becomes X01, X03, X02: the equal-quantity items keep their starting order.

Now read the IDs. They are not ascending, so this list does not meet the precondition for ID binary search. Keep a separate ID-ordered view or use a dictionary for repeated unique-ID lookup. Keep the quantity-ordered view for display.

For one search in unsorted data, linear search avoids sorting first. For repeated searches, compare the preparation and update costs before choosing binary search.

Trace empty input, one item, first and last matches, and an absent target. This practice uses a documented result of an index or −1. Check the particular routine’s contract rather than assuming every search uses the same failure result.

For Equipment subclasses, identify common state/behaviour, overriding and polymorphic calls. Check the stock invariant after a rejected loan and after a repeated return. A changed rejection message needs regression evidence that valid loans and stock behaviour still work; component success alone is not complete acceptance evidence.

Visual walkthrough

Quantity order is not ID order

Stable insertion sort by quantity turns X03:4, X01:2, X02:4 into these positions.

Pause and predict: Can you binary-search this array directly for ID X02 using ascending ID comparisons?

Show the explanation

No. The ID order X01, X03, X02 is not ascending. The quantity order does not meet the ID-search precondition.

Try a small change: Build an ascending-ID view. Explain how it can coexist with this quantity-ordered display without changing the original purpose of either view.

5. Transfer subnet and performance reasoning

Work a new host: 192.168.60.130/28. Show mask, aligned network, broadcast, ordinary host range and capacity before selecting a gateway. Then decide whether destination .145 belongs to the same prefix.

CheckExplained result
Mask / block size255.255.255.240 /16 addresses
Network / broadcast192.168.60.128 /192.168.60.143
Ordinary hosts / capacity.129–.142 /14
Candidate gateway.129, provided it is an actual reachable router interface and not duplicated
Destination .145Different prefix: .144/28
Nine endpoints + gateway10 usable needed; /29 gives 6, /28 gives 14

For a remote destination with no NAT, keep the remote IP destination but send the local frame to the gateway MAC. Separate layer 2 switching from layer 3 routing. IPv6 remains 128-bit hexadecimal notation; IPv4 network/broadcast subtraction is not its general allocation rule.

Sixteen clients at 6 Mbit/s need 96 Mbit/s. A 100 Mbit/s uplink fits the stated ideal demand with only 4 Mbit/s spare before overhead or other traffic. A 300 MB file at 80 Mbit/s has a 30-second ideal minimum. Explain why nominal capacity alone cannot promise the real result.

6. Evaluate a network answer against evidence

A design places Staff and Visitors in different VLANs, enables routing between them and adds no filtering. Explain why it has not enforced the guest restriction. Place service-specific rules at a relevant routing boundary, test allowed and denied initiation, and consider paths that bypass it. DNS/DHCP and authorised management dependencies still need narrow treatment.

If ping works but web fails, investigate the service, transport policy and application/TLS conditions. If traceroute has an unanswered intermediate hop but later replies, record that missing response without declaring the link broken. Ping does not measure bulk throughput or prove every service works.

Use a Cisco-convention diagram with intermediary/end devices, prefixes, gateway roles, link labels and a policy boundary. Synthetic scenarios are adequate for reasoning practice, but teacher-assigned live ping/traceroute practice and diagram symbol fidelity remain separate evidence requirements.

7. Attempt fresh mixed transfer

Lesson 3 uses a fresh mixed task before answers are shown. The workbook supplies different IDs, a /27 subnet, a capacity limit and a software test requirement. Allow roughly 25 minutes for the attempt, then compare with the explanations and use remaining time for corrections. This is optional, ungraded practice; it is not an official examination-format example.

Download consolidation pack · Student workbook · Explained answers · Python starter. The pack includes station cards, teacher reference code and a revision-plan CSV. Teacher files are separate, not access-protected.

8. Build an evidence-based revision plan

In lesson 4, complete one delayed retry for each selected priority and a short mixed check. Record the outcome, help used and remaining uncertainty. A successful repetition immediately after reading an answer is useful practice, but weaker evidence than an independent fresh attempt later.

Plan week 16 exam preparation from specific needs: task, reason, resource, time and success evidence. Keep unresolved practical skills visible. Avoid recording mastery merely because a page was read or a model output matched a prediction.

Earlier resources: integrated review, sorting, inheritance, subnetting and network design. Technical reference: Python data structures. Curriculum: 2026 SCSA Year 12 syllabus. Questions and explanations are original drafts for classroom review.

9. Transfer traversal to a fresh map

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. The code is ordinary Python 3 and runs offline. Work in a disposable learning folder. These are ungraded practice examples, not additional assessment requirements.

Record the input or initial state, expected outcome, actual outcome, pass/fail and a reason. Where an invalid input is outside the function's stated contract, explain that precondition rather than silently inventing behaviour.

Pause and predict

Does an empty grid have any wall tiles?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download grid_transfer.py

def count_walls(grid):
    total = 0
    for row in grid:
        for tile in row:
            if tile == 1:
                total += 1
    return total
for grid in [[], [[0]], [[1, 0], [1, 1]]]:
    print(count_walls(grid))
Show expected output after your prediction
0
0
3

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Complete a row-by-row trace and add an all-floor grid before checking output.
  2. Independent transfer: Create one new normal case, one boundary/empty case and one missing/invalid case relevant to this example. State any preconditions. Predict independently, run, explain the first mismatch if present, and keep the cases for regression after your change.
  3. Delayed retrieval: After a gap, solve a changed version without copying the example. Explain one design decision and use a new test to demonstrate transfer.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The outputs are 0, 0 and 3. Each matching tile is counted once; row count alone is not the wall count.

Practice and explain

COPY

Why can a copied dictionary still share a list value?

Show explained answer

The mapping copy is shallow: it copies references to values. Appending to a shared nested list is visible through both mappings.

SEARCH

Is X01,X03,X02 suitable for binary search by ID?

Show explained answer

No. IDs are not ascending. Use a correctly ordered ID view or another suitable search structure.

CAPACITY

Does 96 Mbit/s demand on a 100 Mbit/s link guarantee success?

Show explained answer

No. It fits the ideal arithmetic, with only 4 Mbit/s spare; overhead/other traffic/endpoint limits still matter.

SUBNET

What subnet contains 192.168.60.130/28?

Show explained answer

192.168.60.128/28; broadcast .143, ordinary hosts .129–.142, 14 usable.

POLICY

Separate VLANs with unrestricted routing: are guests isolated from staff?

Show explained answer

Layer 2 broadcast domains are separate, but routed traffic can pass. Enforce and test the required inter-zone policy.

EVIDENCE

What is stronger than rereading the answer and repeating it immediately?

Show explained answer

An independent fresh question later, with reasoning and a recorded result; use it to check transfer and retention.

Your practical task

Choose one programming and one networking priority, complete the matching station cards, attempt the fresh mixed transfer and record a delayed retry. Produce a revision plan with two concrete next actions and practical evidence still outstanding.

Show illustrative answer / example

Use the error log to justify priorities. Dictionary copy is shallow; sorting and searching keys must agree. For .130/28: network .128, broadcast .143, 14 ordinary usable addresses. A demand of 96 Mbit/s fits 100 Mbit/s ideally but does not guarantee throughput. A network restriction requires actual policy enforcement and evidence. Record a fresh independent retry for each priority.

Chapter recap

Consolidation turns a broad weakness into a specific correction and a fresh demonstration. Keep assumptions, evidence and unresolved skills visible as you prepare for week 16.

  2. Lesson 2: two targeted stations, teacher feedback and explained correction; extensions for secure skills.
  3. Lesson 3: fresh mixed transfer, self-review and correction within the same lesson.
  4. Lesson 4: delayed retries, mixed retrieval and a concrete week 16 revision plan. Four lessons in week 15; no additional project.

1. Understand the scope of this preparation

Use the four week 16 lessons to practice Unit 3. The official Year 12 ATAR examination samples both Units 3 and 4, so these original exercises cover only part of the full course.

Follow your school’s assessment instructions for any actual examination. These resources do not replace a full-course paper.

The verified 2026 design brief allows 10 minutes of reading and 3 hours of working time. It divides the paper as follows:

  • Short answer: 40%, 20–30 questions, with a suggested 70 minutes.
  • Extended answer: 60%, 4–6 questions, with a suggested 110 minutes.

Check the current SCSA instructions and your school’s directions before an actual assessment.

SCSA 2026 Year 12 syllabus and examination design brief. The pack below deliberately uses a shorter classroom format and ungraded questions.

2. Read the task and plan the evidence

Read the whole question before answering. Identify the command word, scenario limits, available marks and required form of evidence. A later part may state an assumption you need.

  • Trace: show how the state changes, step by step.
  • Explain: give the mechanism or reason.
  • Justify: connect your choice to the requirements.
  • Evaluate: weigh evidence, alternatives and limitations.
Question typeUseful evidence
Code traceVariable/index/state table and final output
Algorithm choicePrecondition, data key/order, preparation/update cost
Software testingInput, expected result, actual result and invariant
Subnet calculationMask, aligned boundary, range, capacity and gateway caveat
Network evaluationDiagram/policy/path, units, observed evidence and limits

Plan your time around the task’s demands and marks, and leave time to check. If you get stuck, show the method you have reached, move on, then return.

Use a reading period only as the supervisor permits. Classroom practice rules do not replace the instructions for an actual examination.

3. Practice a trace and a contract

stock = {"A01": 2, "A02": 1}
snapshot = stock.copy()
for key in ["A01", "A02", "A01"]:
    if stock[key] > 0:
        stock[key] -= 1
print(stock)
print(snapshot)

Trace each requested key as the code runs. The successful updates leave A01 and A02 at zero. The snapshot keeps the starting integer values because it is a separate mapping.

A snapshot records values at a particular point; it is not a live view of later changes. Here the integers are immutable. Explain why a shallow copy with mutable list values would still share those lists.

Before writing available_ids(records), state its contract:

  • What input is valid?
  • What order must the result use?
  • What does it return?
  • May it change the input?

Here, return IDs with positive quantities in input order, leaving out zero quantities. Test an empty collection, all-zero quantities and mixed quantities.

Add checks for malformed data only if the requirement asks for them. Extra validation must not silently change the agreed behaviour.

4. Attempt the original timed practice

The downloadable practice has eight short tasks and two extended tasks. Try them at your own pace, or use 40 minutes as an optional pacing exercise. These original questions are ungraded, sample Unit 3 only, and do not predict the official examination.

Lesson 1 rehearses reading, pacing and a worked trace. Lesson 2 contains the complete practice attempt with time left for an initial reflection. Lesson 3 is self-review and targeted correction; lesson 4 is fresh retries and final readiness checks. There is no additional project or extra examination scheduled inside these lessons.

5. Mark the method and diagnose the error

Compare your reasoning with the explanations; equivalent correct methods are welcome. Separate missing knowledge, failed preconditions, arithmetic/unit errors, unclear explanations and time-management issues. Check that each claim is supported by your written reasoning.

For a network calculation, show address bits or block boundaries and verify alignment/capacity. For a policy answer, identify actual filtering and dependencies rather than assuming private addresses or VLAN labels provide security. For a diagnostic answer, do not claim a ping reply proves the web service or that an unanswered traceroute probe proves a broken hop.

Rewrite two answers that need clearer reasoning with the missing evidence, then solve the pack’s different-value retry without the guide. Keep the attempt, correction and retry result together.

6. Use a fresh retry to check transfer

Fresh case: host 192.168.100.82/28. Find network, broadcast, ordinary range and a gateway candidate. Compare 12 clients at 7 Mbit/s with a 100 Mbit/s uplink, then estimate 250 MB at 80 Mbit/s. Explain why an ideal fit is not measured throughput.

Compare after attempting

Network .80, broadcast .95, hosts .81–.94, 14 usable; .81 is a mathematical gateway candidate, subject to actual router configuration and no duplicate. Demand 84 Mbit/s fits 100 ideally with 16 Mbit/s spare; 250 × 8 ÷ 80 = 25 seconds ideally.

Programming retry: B01:0,B02:3,B03:0,B04:1 should produce B02,B04 without modifying input. Explain search/key ordering separately from a quantity-ordered display. Use previous sorting, object and network-model packs for priorities not represented in this small sample.

7. Complete the final readiness check

Check that you can explain and apply data structures, search/sort contracts, object behaviour and reliable testing; address prefixes/ranges; layer/address roles; network components, segmentation, capacity and evidence limits. Use the week 15 plan for any remaining priority. Make a manageable final plan rather than introducing new project features.

Confirm school-specific assessment instructions, permitted equipment and arrangements with the teacher. Written practice cannot stand in for any outstanding live-tool or practical evidence. Unit 3 editorial coverage, Cisco symbol fidelity, independent teacher review and classroom evidence still need checking before claiming complete coverage.

8. Write a trace and state the precondition

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. The code is ordinary Python 3 and runs offline. Work in a disposable learning folder. These are ungraded practice examples, not additional assessment requirements.

Record the input or initial state, expected outcome, actual outcome, pass/fail and a reason. Where an invalid input is outside the function's stated contract, explain that precondition rather than silently inventing behaviour.

Pause and predict

Which bounds change after each non-matching midpoint?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download binary_search_checks.py

def binary_search(values, target):
    # Contract: values are sorted in ascending order.
    low, high = 0, len(values) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if values[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if values[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1
for target in [2, 8, 14, 9]:
    print(target, binary_search([2, 5, 8, 11, 14], target))
print("empty", binary_search([], 2))
Show expected output after your prediction
2 0
8 2
14 4
9 -1
empty -1

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Trace target 9 without running, then justify why discarding half is valid only for ordered data.
  2. Independent transfer: Create one new normal case, one boundary/empty case and one missing/invalid case relevant to this example. State any preconditions. Predict independently, run, explain the first mismatch if present, and keep the cases for regression after your change.
  3. Delayed retrieval: After a gap, solve a changed version without copying the example. Explain one design decision and use a new test to demonstrate transfer.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The search returns -1 for 9. Explain the interval invariant and compare with a fresh missing target such as 3.

Practice and explain

CONTRACT

Should available_ids reorder records by quantity?

Show explained answer

No. Its contract requires input order and no mutation; sorting changes the required behaviour.

TIME

Is this optional classroom practice the official examination format?

Show explained answer

No. It is a shorter formative Unit 3 sample; the Year 12 examination covers Units 3 and 4 under the current SCSA brief.

SUBNET

Why show the mask and boundary calculation rather than only a final network?

Show explained answer

It supports the method, lets you verify alignment and makes an arithmetic error easier to diagnose.

EVIDENCE

Does rewriting the explained answer guide prove transfer?

Show explained answer

No. Attempt a new case independently and record its result.

POLICY

What is missing from saying “Guests have another VLAN, therefore secure”?

Show explained answer

Routing/filtering enforcement, allowed services/dependencies, bypass considerations and positive/negative test evidence.

Your practical task

Complete the stimulus and optional mixed practice under the classroom timing, compare your reasoning with the explained answers, correct two errors and attempt fresh programming/network retries. Complete a final readiness checklist and identify any practical or coverage evidence still pending.

Show illustrative answer / example

Follow the separate explained answer guide. Trace stock to zero while the snapshot retains 2 and 1; available_ids preserves positive-quantity IDs in input order. Network answers must show prefixes, ranges and actual policy enforcement. The fresh case .82/28 belongs to .80/28 with 14 ordinary usable addresses; 84 Mbit/s fits 100 Mbit/s ideally, and 250 MB at 80 Mbit/s takes 25 seconds ideally.

Chapter recap

Preparation is an attempt, a diagnosis and a fresh demonstration. Write the method, match the contract and state what the evidence can support. Keep full-course and school assessment instructions distinct from this classroom sample.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: assessment scope, commands, pacing and worked trace/contract rehearsal.
  2. Lesson 2: teacher setup, 40-minute original practice and initial reflection.
  3. Lesson 3: explained self-review, error diagnosis and targeted correction.
  4. Lesson 4: fresh independent retries, final readiness checklist and revision plan. Four lessons in week 16; weeks 17–18 remain blocked for examinations.
